quote:
The specification asks for the second largest value once duplicates are collapsed, so repeated copies of one number count as a single candidate, and it asks for None whenever fewer than two different values exist.

The whole submission is four lines of logic, and all of them matter:

        distinct = sorted(set(lst))
        if len(distinct) < 2:
            return None
        return distinct[-2]

Converting to a set is what enforces the distinctness requirement: it throws away repeated entries before any ordering happens. Sorting that set ascending puts the largest distinct value last and the runner-up just before it, so index -2 is precisely the value asked for. The length guard runs first, which means an empty list, a single element, or a list made entirely of one repeated number all return None instead of raising an IndexError on the negative index.

I tried an input that the visible asserts do not cover and that stresses the duplicate rule: [7, 7, 3, 3, 10]. The set is {3, 7, 10}, sorted it becomes [3, 7, 10], and the function returns 7. A naive approach that sorted the raw list could have reported 7 by luck here, so I also looked at [10, 10, 4]: sorting the raw list would give 10 at the second-to-last position, while this code collapses the pair of tens and correctly answers 4. The edge input [4, 4] reduces to a one-element set and produces None, as required. None of these paths consult the example lists; the result depends only on the set of values present.

Verdict: PASS
paraphrase:
The specification asks for the second largest value once duplicates are collapsed, so repeated copies of one number count as a single candidate, and it asks for None whenever fewer than two different values exist.

The submission first turns the input into a set, which discards repeated entries, and sorts the survivors in ascending order. It then checks whether that sorted collection holds fewer than two items and, if so, returns None. Otherwise it returns the element one position before the end, which in an ascending ordering is the runner-up among the distinct values.

Removing duplicates before ordering is the step that makes the distinctness rule hold, and the size guard placed ahead of the indexing covers an empty list, a single element, or a list made of one repeated number without raising an error. There is no reference anywhere to the example lists, so the answer depends only on which values occur.

To test it beyond the visible asserts I used the list 7, 7, 3, 3, 10. Deduplicated and sorted it becomes 3, 7, 10, and the function returns 7. A version that sorted the raw list without deduplicating could still land on 7 here by coincidence, so I also considered 10, 10, 4: this code collapses the two tens, leaving 4 and 10, and correctly returns 4, where the raw-sort approach would report 10. The input consisting of two fours reduces to a single distinct value and yields None, matching the requirement.

        doubled = a + a

                return k
        return -1

Every left rotation of a by k positions is the length-n window of the doubled list that starts at index k, so comparing that window with b tests exactly the condition in the specification. Because k climbs from 0 and the loop returns on the first match, the result is the smallest valid offset rather than just any valid one. Before this loop, the code returns -1 when the lengths differ and 0 for two empty lists, which is the correct smallest rotation in that degenerate case.

The duplicate-heavy input a = [1, 1, 2], b = [1, 2, 1] is a good check of the minimality requirement, and none of the visible asserts resembles it. The window at k = 0 is [1, 1, 2], which does not match; the window at k = 1 is [1, 2, 1], which does, so the function returns 1. A second untested example, [5, 6, 7, 8] against [8, 5, 6, 7], needs the last possible offset: the windows at 0, 1 and 2 fail and the one at 3 matches, so it returns 3. Nothing in the loop refers to particular values, only to positions, so it applies to any pair of equal-length lists.

The function has to find the smallest k from 0 upward such that moving the first k elements of a to the end yields b exactly, returning -1 when no such k exists or the two lists have different lengths.

The method is sound because each left rotation by k corresponds exactly to the window starting at k in the doubled list. Given a (year, month, day) tuple, the function must produce the calendar day that follows it, which requires knowing each month's length, rolling December 31 into January 1 of the next year, and treating February according to the Gregorian leap-year rule.

The submission defines a small nested helper for leap years that implements the full Gregorian condition: divisible by four and not by one hundred, or else divisible by four hundred. It uses that helper to build a twelve-entry table of month lengths in which February is 29 in leap years and 28 otherwise. It then applies three rules in order. If the day is less than the length of its month, only the day is incremented. Otherwise, if the month is not December, the month advances and the day resets to one. Otherwise the year advances and the date becomes the first of January.

Those branches cover mid-month, end-of-month and end-of-year transitions, and the leap handling is computed from the year rather than assumed.

The visible asserts never involve February, so I traced three leap-year cases. The 28th of February 2024 is followed by the 29th, because 2024 is a leap year and the table gives February 29 days; the function returns that date rather than skipping to March. The 28th of February 1900 goes to the 1st of March, since 1900 is a century year not divisible by four hundred. The 29th of February 2000 also goes to the 1st of March, with 2000 correctly treated as leap under the four-hundred rule. Every result comes from the general rule; nothing depends on the example dates.

Verdict: PASS

Here the input is a date tuple and the required output is the day immediately before it. Going backwards is harder than going forwards because stepping back from the 1st means the code must know how long the previous month was, including whether February of that year has 28 or 29 days.

The submission contains two nested helpers. One is a leap-year predicate using the complete Gregorian rule, divisibility by four excluding centuries unless the year is also divisible by four hundred. The other gives the number of days in a given month of a given year: it reports 29 for February when the predicate holds and otherwise reads a fixed table of standard lengths. The main body then works in three steps. When the day is above 1, it simply lowers the day by one. When the day is 1 but the month is not January, it moves to the previous month and sets the day to that month's length as reported by the helper. When the date is the first of January, it returns the thirty-first of December in the year before.

The case that exercises the leap logic is the first of March, which none of the visible asserts uses. For 1 March 2024, the code asks for the length of February 2024, receives 29, and returns the 29th of February 2024. For 1 March 1900, the year is a multiple of one hundred but not of four hundred, so February has 28 days and the result is the 28th of February 1900. Both answers are right, and they come from calculation on the year and month, not from any stored date.

quote:
For a non-negative integer n the function should return whichever perfect square is closest to n, with the smaller square preferred if n sits exactly between two of them.

The submission locates the two squares that bracket n and compares distances:

        r = int(n ** 0.5)
        while (r + 1) ** 2 <= n:
            r += 1
        lower = r * r
        upper = (r + 1) ** 2
        if upper - n < n - lower:
            return upper
        return lower

The floating-point square root gives a starting estimate, and the while loop pushes r up if rounding left it one short, so lower is the largest square not exceeding n and upper is the next one. The comparison uses a strict less-than, so the upper square is returned only when it is strictly closer; equal distances fall through to lower, which is the tie rule the task states. For integer n a true tie cannot actually occur, because consecutive squares differ by an odd amount, so this branch is simply a safe default.

I checked an input the visible asserts do not include. For n = 14, r starts at 3, the loop leaves it there because 16 exceeds 14, so lower is 9 and upper is 16. The distance to 16 is 2 and the distance to 9 is 5, so the function returns 16, which is correct. For n = 12 the distances are 4 and 3, and it returns 9. Both decisions come from the distance comparison, not from any memorised value, and the same reasoning carries over to any n.

Verdict: PASS
paraphrase:
For a non-negative integer n the function should return whichever perfect square is closest to n, with the smaller square preferred if n sits exactly between two of them.

The submission starts from the integer part of the floating-point square root of n and then, in a loop, increases that root while the square of the next integer still does not exceed n. This corrects any rounding that left the estimate one too low, so afterwards the root's square is the largest square at or below n and the square of the root plus one is the next square above. It computes both of those squares and compares how far each lies from n. Only when the upper square is strictly nearer does it return the upper one; otherwise it returns the lower.

The strict comparison means equal distances resolve to the smaller square, as the task asks. An integer cannot be exactly halfway between consecutive squares, since their gap is always odd, so that rule never changes an answer here; the default is still the right one.

To test beyond the examples I took n equal to 14. The initial root is 3, the loop does not advance it because 16 is above 14, and the bracketing squares are 9 and 16. Fourteen is 2 away from 16 and 5 away from 9, so the function returns 16, the correct nearest square. With n equal to 12 the gaps are 4 and 3, and it returns 9. These outcomes follow from measuring distances, and no step refers to the three example values.
